https://catholicphilly.com/2026/07/news/.text: Archdiocese of Philadelphia Get our newsletter Advertise with us Archdiocese of Philadelphia Get our newsletter Advertise with us News Local News Catholic Education Catholic Charities of Philadelphia People and Events Sports Obituaries Calendar of Events Submit your event USCCB News and Statements Vatican News Features Photo Features Video Features Commentaries Catholic Spirituality Podcasts Profile Hispanic Catholics Archbishop Pérez’s Messages Catholic Directory Support Our Work Newsletter Signup About Us St. Charles Seminary Receives $1 Million Anonymous Gift to Support Endowment Kevin Williams Retires From ‘Job Well Done’ for 46 Years Serving Seniors Archbishop Pérez Asks for Prayers Ahead of Days for Educators How the 1976 Eucharistic Congress Put Catholic Diversity on Display Handmaids of the Sacred Heart Mark 100 Years of Sharing ‘Joyful Love’ Archdiocesan High Schools, Teachers Union Ratify New Three-Year Contract 41 ‘Pierogi Pilgrims’ from Philadelphia Find God in Poland’s Holy Sites By Jay Sorgi • Posted July 31, 2026 More than 40 young Philadelphians traveled to Poland July 2-12 on a pilgrimage seeking God. They found the Lord in expected and unexpected places, with poignance from lost loved ones, in persistent symbols of faith that rebuilt a nation, and in the unabashed joy of a surprise engagement and future matrimony. Pauline Father Timothy Tarnacki, the director of the archdiocesan Office for Ministry with Young Adults (OMYA), took 41 Catholics on the pilgrimage themed “We Want God!” to a series of holy sites and other stops in Poland, a nation long-defined and even reborn through the Catholic faith that permeates within the Eastern European land. “With the pilgrimage design and Father Timothy’s guidance, we really saw how connected faith and culture, and truly everything is in Poland,” pilgrim Mairwen Minson said. “We visited religious sites and historical sites, but really all of them were religious. The faith is so built into Poland and it is a gift to see that.” Each participant received a 102-page journal filled with related Saints of the Day plus daily Mass readings accompanying the liturgies they would encounter during the pilgrimage. Father Tarnacki, a native of Poland who came to the United States as a boy, says the journey was not about himself but about God touching the lives of the assembled young adults under 40 years old who came with him. Yet it was impossible for him to not be touched by how he brought new friends from across an ocean to places that have deeply touched his own faith life. That includes Jasna Góra, the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Częstochowa that houses the original Black Madonna icon, and its attached monastery in Częstochowa that was part of his own pathway with the Pauline Fathers. “That is the heart of Polish spirituality, and I spent every summer there,” he said. “Throughout the year, we would be very often sent there to minister at the shrine. That’s such a big part of my formation and the charism of my community.” Laura Lindmeier encountered the day of a lifetime beside that Black Madonna icon. “The icon itself tells the story of the Polish people whose deep devotion has been tied to a history of deep suffering,” said Lindmeier, whose spiritual journey has often been anchored at the National Shrine of Our Lady of Czestochowa in Doylestown. “I encountered Our Lady’s tenderness in a new way,” she added. “Our group had the privilege of celebrating a private Mass in the chapel which houses the original miraculous icon.” Then after she helped lead music for the Mass with her boyfriend, Alvaro, the blessed surprise of a lifetime happened. “Álvaro got down on one knee and proposed immediately after the Mass had finished!” she said. “I was absolutely floored! Father Timothy’s homily that day spoke of the icon and the loving gaze of Our Lady over unique moments in our life. I felt this so clearly. Beneath her gaze, I said yes to my vocation with profound peace and joy, a vocation which promises to hold tenderness and suffering ever in tension, just as she does.” Father Tarnacki plans on being a celebrant for their wedding. Pilgrims traveled to the Sanctuary of the Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Giertzwald, the Shrine of St. Faustina and the Tomb of Blessed Jerzy Popiełuszko in Warsaw, the location in Krakow where St. Stanislaus was martyred, the city of Wadowice where St. John Paul II was born and where a museum is dedicated to him, and the city’s Our Lady of the Calvary Shrine, and then a return to Krakow with a Mass at the Chapel of the Tomb of St. Faustina. “I had been struggling to talk to Mary because of some losses,” Minson said. “Going to Giertzwald, the Marian apparition site, was both the hardest and best day of the pilgrimage for me. I genuinely wanted to hide from my pain and Mary’s presence, but with the group there, I stayed and had such a healing conversation with Mary. It was incredible, to sob and get through my grief with Mary there guiding me through what I needed.” The pilgrimage also included time marking how totalitarianism attempted to drown the Catholic faith, from fascism in World War II to communism during the Cold War era. In both cases, the Church more than survived — it served as the response. The young adults saw both the horrors of the Nazi concentration and extermination camp at Auschwitz-Birkenau, and the hope and joy of the European Solidarity Centre in Gdansk, a city of the Catholic-inspired Solidarity resistance to the Soviet bloc rule of Poland at the time. “We remembered the story of St. Maximilian Kolbe as we visited the starvation bunker that served as the place of his martyrdom,” Lindmeier said of the saint’s willingness to give his life for another person at Auschwitz. “St. Maximilian Kolbe, in imitation of Christ, proves that sacrificial love is what gives these gifts their staying power and why they are worthy of laying down one’s life.” Colleen Flannery, who has Polish heritage, saw many examples of the resilience of the Polish people, deeply imbued within the Catholic faith. “We were on the pilgrimage over the Fourth of July holiday, and it felt so different not being home, but being abroad helped me to see freedom through a different lens,” she said. “It put into perspective how precious freedom is, and how important it is to safeguard and not take it for granted.” Andrea Maychak celebrated a birthday that led to a most Polish, and appropriate, surprise. Father Tarnacki “surprised me with the most appropriate birthday presents: a pierogi pillow paired with a third class relic of Pope John Paul II,” she said. “I joked the rest of the trip that I was a ‘pierogi pilgrim!’’’ The 41 who came from Philadelphia returned with more than pierogis. Father Tarnacki believes they came back changed. “It’s just amazing to see how the Lord works in these kinds of pilgrimages, because the pilgrimage is all about transformation,” he said. “It’s all about encountering God on the way, and I think that’s what has been happening through the Holy Spirit.” Join the CatholicPhilly.com family CatholicPhilly.com works to strengthen the connections between people, families and communities every day by delivering the news people need to know about the Catholic Church, especially in the Philadelphia region, and the world in which we live. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/17/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter motorcsónakból biztosít mindenkit, hogy jól halad a fenékküszöb építése Paksnál Belföld Csurgó Dénes Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Ismét élőben jelentkezett be Paksról, a fenékküszöb építésének munkálatairól Magyar Péter miniszterelnök, aki a védekezést és építkezést vezető szakemberekkel együtt előbb a partról, majd csónakba szállva a vízről mutatta meg, hogy haladnak a munkálatok Paksnál. Mint Magyar elmondta, folyamatosan zajlik a munka, 0-24-ben építik a vízszint emelését szolgáló fenékküszöböt és süllyesztik be azt a két bárkát, amelyekkel szintén a vízszintet szeretnék emelni, hogy az alacsony vízállás miatt ne kerüljön veszélybe a paksi atomerőmű termelése, így az ország energiabiztonsága. A kormányfő hangsúlyozta, hogy múlt hét szerdán döntött a kormány a fenékküszöb építéséről és a bárkák besüllyesztéséről, most, 5 nappal később pedig már egészen másképp néz ki a Dunának ez a szakasza és jól haladnak a munkálatok. „Kisebb noszogatásra”, de egészen távoli bányákból is ajánlottak fel követ, amiből több ezer tonnára van még szükség a munkák elvégzéséhez. A felajánlott mennyiség elegendő lesz a szakemberek szerint, a szűk keresztmetszet a szállítás, nincs elég sofőr, aki gyorsan el tudja hozni a rakományt, a vasúti szállítás pedig napokkal hosszabbítaná meg a folyamatot. A paksi építkezés mellett a Ráckevei-Soroksári Dunaág zsilipjének megnyitásával is tudják növelni a szakemberek a vízszintet, egy másodpercenként 20 köbméterrel növeli a vízmennyiséget a folyóban. Ennek ellenére szerdáig még várhatóan apadni fog a Duna vízszintje, de valószínűleg az eddigi intézkedésekkel olyan szinten lehet tartani a vízszintet Paksnál, hogy a két működő turbina továbbra is biztonságosan tudjon áramot termelni. Magyar Péter szerint pedig szerdától már emelkedhet a Duna vízszintje, mert a folyó osztrák és német vízgyűjtő területein is esik, jövő héttől pedig akár 40 centivel is emelkedhet a vízszint a mostanihoz képest. Ha ez bekövetkezik, akkor elindulhat a két leállított paksi turbina ütemezett visszakapcsolása is, hogy az ország legfontosabb erőműve teljes kapacitáson termelhessen. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8m.text: Image source, DSNS / Ukraine Image caption, The building in Kyiv housing the Ukrainian TV channel We are Ukraine partially collapsed after the Russian strike By Claire Keenan Â and Â Jaroslav Lukiv Published 8 September 2026, 11:23 BST Updated 3 hours ago A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Zelensky said the daytime attack was a "new page in Russian degradation", while photos shared by the president showed a partially collapsed building. At least five people have been killed in overnight and daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv. A separate attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee, officials have said. Both countries had earlier agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend. Referring to Tuesday's Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian TV channel We Are Ukraine, Zelensky said: "Today, Russia carried out a strike on the media, journalists. "Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts," he added in a renewed plea to Ukraine's allies in Europe, the US and around the world. We Are Ukraine has published footage which it says shows the moment the drone hit its newsroom. "The footage confirms that this was not an accidental strike, but a deliberate attack targeting journalists," the channel said in a post on Telegram. A BBC team later visited the site, confirming that the TV channel's newsroom was damaged in the strike, which reportedly interrupted the live broadcast. Earlier on Tuesday, air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces carried out missile and drone strikes on Kyiv, the local authorities said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Kyiv residents took shelter in underground metro stations during overnight Russian drone and missile strikes A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed three people and injured another 25, the state emergencies service DSNS said. Residential buildings were hit, including a five-storey house in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district. People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war. By Tuesday afternoon, the death toll had reached five people. According to a BBC Verify analysis , Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said early on Tuesday. The talks with Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv ended without any major breakthroughs. On Tuesday evening, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a "constructive and very frank" talks on the phone, Moscow said. The two leaders spoke for an hour, Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said. The Trump administration has not publicly commented, while Witkoff earlier had said that "substantive progress was made", without giving any further details. Ushakov had said on Saturday that Trump's envoys were informed in Moscow about "the significant advances made by the Russian armed forces" on the battlefield and stressed that the Kremlin's "set objectives would be achieved". Meanwhile, Zelensky said he expected the war to continue into the winter after meeting Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv on Sunday - their first ever visit to Ukraine. Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US. Putin has so far showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: Russia has once again entered Polish airspace with warplanes launched to intercept. The incident happened just after 11am local time in the north of the town of Braniewo, northern Poland. The Polish Operational Command of the Armed Forces explained a Russian Mi-8 Armed Forces helicopter conducted a "brief violation" of the Polish airspace. The aircraft was conducting a flight from the Kaliningrad Oblast and remained in Poland for 42 seconds. A statement from the Polish Operational Command released just after 12.30pm BST reads: "We inform that on September 23 this year at 11:08 a.m., north of the town of Braniewo, there was a brief violation of the airspace of the Republic of Poland by an Mi-8 helicopter of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation. "The helicopter was conducting a flight from the Kaliningrad Oblast. It violated Polish airspace to a maximum depth of approximately 300 m and remained in it for 42 seconds. "The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Poland. Fighter aircraft were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby. "The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence. The crews of the Republic of Poland's air defence systems conduct round-the-clock observation, remaining in constant readiness to ensure the safety of Polish airspace." This comes as the Polish Operational Command said only this morning that it remained in "constant readiness to ensure the safety of Polish airspace". The announcement was made after military aviation operations were carried out to ensure safety during Russian strikes. The central European country has been on high alert as NATO fighter jets were also scrambled in Poland and Latvia on Monday night after Russian president Vladimir Putin launched an intense attack on Ukraine. Residents in eastern Poland received an emergency alert warning them about the Russian attack on Ukraine. This was the fourth time in seven days that Polish and allied aircraft were sent out due to attacks near the border with Ukraine. Last week, Poland's prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that Russian is planning to strike countries supporting Ukraine and then claim the attacks were "accidental".

https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: BRUSSELS — Donald Trump’s threat to halt U.S. diesel exports could leave Europe’s truckers facing another sharp rise in fuel costs — and consumers paying more for goods. The U.S. president said Wednesday that he is still "thinking about" an export ban as his administration tries to bring down record fuel prices at home. The White House is also checking if European countries could release their diesel reserves to lower prices. More expensive diesel could have a knock-on impact across Europe. "Everything on the shelf will cost more," said Cristina Scarfia, head of European affairs at Italian freight federation Confetra. Advertisement Advertisement Europe has grown increasingly reliant on American diesel after war, shipping disruption and refinery outages sharply reduced supplies from the Middle East and Russia. That reliance is now leaving Europe's truckers exposed in an industry that already runs on thin margins and has little room to absorb another shock. "There is a huge risk of bankruptcies" for small and medium-sized companies, said Scarfia. Larger companies are more likely to survive by charging more for their services, she added. The average EU diesel price reached €2.26 per liter on Sept. 17 — 38% higher than in late February, according to the International Road Transport Union . It's a new record, topping the previous high set during the 2022 energy crisis sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Confetra estimates that a U.S. export ban could push diesel prices in the EU well above €3 per liter, Scarfia said. Running out of options As Middle Eastern exports have fallen following the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, Europe has increasingly turned to the U.S. to fill the gap. American diesel now accounts for roughly half of Europe's seaborne imports, according to IRU figures. If Washington bans those exports, road freight would be especially exposed. David Doherty, head of natural resources research at strategic research provider BloombergNEF, said that logistics is Europe's biggest diesel user. Transport accounts for 77% of EU diesel and gas oil consumption, according to Eurostat . Advertisement Advertisement "There's really limited, at least quick, alternatives there," Doherty said. "You and me can decide to stop driving if the prices get really high and the world is not going to fall apart. If there's no trucks operating around Germany or Poland, the two biggest markets, you'll probably start to see pain points." "The knock-on effects go far beyond just expensive diesel," Doherty said. "It could be no diesel in the right place, it could be long refills, it could be queues." Hours spent waiting for fuel would also eat into the time drivers have left to actually deliver goods. The biggest pressure on trucking companies is likely to be financial. A truck driver fills up his vehicle in Dunkirk, France on March 5, 2018. | Jack Taylor/Getty Images Diesel makes up roughly 30% of the cost of running an international trucking company, according to Jan Buczek, president of Poland's Association of International Road Transport Carriers. If diesel prices climb high enough, some trips simply stop making financial sense — and companies can run out of the cash they need to keep going. Trucking companies have to pay for diesel, wages and tolls up front, Buczek added, but payment from customers for a completed job can take weeks to arrive. A sudden jump in fuel prices could create an immediate cash crunch — meaning bills come due before the money to cover them does. "At diesel prices of around €3 per liter, the risk that some operators go under would be very real, particularly if prices stayed at that level for a prolonged period," Buczek said. Advertisement Advertisement Small and medium-sized companies are the most exposed. They typically have smaller cash reserves, less access to credit and less leverage with customers than large logistics groups — and they'd be heading into a new diesel shock already weakened. More than 1,000 companies have already disappeared from Poland's international trucking market this year, Buczek added. Park the truck For companies that survive, the next question is who pays the higher fuel bill. On the spot market — where a company books a single truck for one shipment rather than signing a longer-term contract — higher diesel prices show up almost immediately. Trucking companies demand higher rates, and if customers won't pay, some trips simply stop making financial sense. "No company can continue providing services below cost for an extended period of time," Buczek said. Trucking companies would likely get pickier about which jobs they take. The first to go would be the lowest-paying ones — routes with long stretches of empty driving, destinations where it's hard to find cargo for the trip back, and jobs that involve long waits to load or unload. "If the cost of providing the service exceeds the revenue generated by it, from the operator's perspective it may be economically more rational to leave the truck parked than to generate another loss," Buczek added. Advertisement Advertisement Scarfia described two likely outcomes. Smaller companies, unable to pass on higher diesel costs, may simply turn down jobs, forcing customers to find someone else. Larger companies are more likely to have contracts that let them add a fuel surcharge — an extra fee tied to the price of diesel — so they can keep moving goods while passing the added cost on to clients. If extremely high prices lasted for weeks, and actual fuel shortages set in too, Buczek said Europe could start to see less trucking capacity on some routes, have trouble finding available trucks, and encounter delays rippling through supply chains. For trucking companies, the impact would be "significant and certainly immediate," said Robin Loos, head of transport and mobility at consumer organization BEUC. "If transport capacity begins to disappear from the market, the consequences very quickly extend beyond the road transport industry itself," Buczek said. At that point, he added, diesel supply will become a matter of "economic security."

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text: The Campaign for Real Ale (Camra) has criticised Andy Burnham and Labour for their attempts to block a bill that would afford extra protections for historic pubs, calling the efforts an “absolute disgrace.” The protections, put forward in a bill by Conservative MP Mike Wood, would have given pubs in England a “legal shield” from unlawful redevelopment, with the 2023 destruction of the Crooked House, which was located in Wood’s Kingswinford and South Staffordshire constituency, cited as an example of what can be avoided.
